candidates.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
candidates.description: Original Study 1a claimed that increasing the magnitude of the vertical distance between a leader and subordinates in an organization chart increases perceived power; this magnitude claim was tested in the current paper's Study 2.
candidates.citation_sentence: Study 2: Following up on ManyLabs' replication failure with an adjusted paradigm of Study 1a, Giessner and Schubert (2007)
candidates.notes: Study 2 found no effect of magnitude of vertical distance while rank order was held constant, and the authors describe the original positive finding as a false positive. The novel rank-order hypothesis is not coded as a separate replication entry.

candidates.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
candidates.description: Original Study 3a claimed that describing a leader as powerful rather than powerless causes participants to place the leader's box higher in an organization chart; this was tested in the current paper's Study 1.
candidates.citation_sentence: In Study 3a of the same original paper (Giessner & Schubert, 2007), we had tested the reverse effect -namely whether describing a leader as powerful versus powerless would result in placing a box of this leader on a higher versus lower vertical position within an organization chart.
candidates.notes: The authors explicitly state that the preregistered Study 1 successfully replicated the main findings of the original study. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

prior_source_review.finding: The matched descriptions target Study 1 (power to placement). Study 2 reverses the causal direction and is not interchangeable even though the original DOI is shared. A genuine type disagreement remains for Study 1.
prior_source_review.evidence:
gistered study successfully replicated the main findings of the original study. Participants placed the box of a leader in a more elevated position when this leader was described as powerful, compared to the condition where the leader was described as having less power. The effect was stronger in this study than in the original study.
